c0006: Average number of events you cater per year, counting every drop-off, buffet, wedding and party. It is the main volume driver of the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, and years 2 and 3 grow in events. Compare it with the capacity row further down.
c0008: EXCL. sales tax, with staffing and the service charge included and the voluntary gratuity left out: the price per guest you quote before tax. Price per guest incl. sales tax = this value × (1 + your sales tax rate). The example sits inside the per-guest range in the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab (Kit estimate); the Pricing Calculator builds a quote per service style; to bring it here, divide its subtotal plus the service charge you keep by the billable guests (its own price per guest excludes the service charge).
c0010: Average number of guests per event across your whole mix, from drop-off lunches for a few dozen people to weddings of over a hundred. A typical event runs 50-75 guests (Kit estimate). Sales per event = guests × price per guest. One cell for the whole workbook: the P&L, break-even and scenarios all read it, so they always agree.
c0012: Growth in events in year 2 over year 1 (enter 0.15 for 15%). Kept conservative on purpose: in its first year a caterer has few repeat clients and referrals, and weddings are booked months ahead.
c0014: Growth in events in year 3 over year 2, kept conservative for the same reason: repeat corporate clients and planner referrals build up slowly.
c0022: Cost of goods sold on food sales. The example (30%) sits inside the 28-35% range for caterers in the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab; the menu matters (a drop-off sandwich lunch runs lower than a carving station). It is the most sensitive lever in the plan: test it at the top of the range before you trust the result.
c0024: Coffee, iced tea, lemonade and soft drinks served with the menu: a high-margin line, set below the food rate. There is no alcohol in this line: the client buys it separately.
c0026: Disposable plates, cutlery, napkins and containers for drop-off orders, as a % of sales. It sits next to cost of goods sold instead of hiding in miscellaneous. Some cities restrict foam and single-use plastics, so check your local rules.
c0028: Share of your sales that comes through corporate catering marketplaces such as ezCater, rather than from clients who book you directly. Set it to 0 if you only sell direct. The marketplace sends you the order but keeps a commission (next row).
c0030: Commission the marketplace keeps on those sales. ezCater charges about 15% on food and delivery (Kit estimate); fees change, so check the current schedule when you sign up. Not used while the marketplace share is 0%.
c0032: Card and ACH fees on total sales. Many companies pay by ACH or check, which lowers the cost; cards cost more. The example (2.5%) is a blended rate: a percentage plus a per-transaction fee, which weighs more on small invoices. Check your processor's statement and enter your effective rate (Kit estimate).
c0042: Monthly cost of your commissary kitchen (hours + storage) and the van's parking spot: one cell for everything you pay the kitchen. The deposit and the months before opening are calculated from it. Shared kitchens charge roughly 15-45 per hour (The Food Corridor, 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey): multiply by your prep hours and add storage and parking. A permitted commissary is required: catering from a home kitchen is not allowed, and cottage food rules do not cover it. Get quotes in your area before you sign.
c0044: Months of deposit on the commissary agreement. Many shared kitchens ask for one month up front: far less than the deposit on a commercial lease. Negotiate it in the written agreement.
c0046: Fuel for the generator and the portable burners, plus water and utility costs that the commissary fee does not cover. It is the one cell for this cost, so you change it in one place and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0048: General liability (venues and planners often require 1M per occurrence), commercial auto for the van and liquor liability for events where bartenders pour the client's alcohol. Insureon publishes averages for small businesses (see the benchmarks table on the "Instructions" tab); the example is a Kit estimate, so get quotes from an insurance agent. It is counted once, as an annual expense, not also in startup costs.
c0050: Van fuel to drive to venues, plus a cushion for unbudgeted running costs. It is a VARIABLE cost: it rises and falls with the number of events, so it cannot sit among the fixed costs or it would move the break-even without anyone noticing.
c0053: Your own money. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection (often around 10% for SBA start-ups; many want 20-30%) on the total cash needed in this plan.
c0055: Principal requested: bank or SBA 7(a). If your loan is an SBA 7(a), this is the cell. It is the only loan that the amortization schedule, the P&L interest and the DSCR use. The "Financing" tab checks that the sources of funds match the total cash needed on the "Startup Costs" tab (which includes working capital and the van and fit-out contingency): copy the loan suggested there into this cell until the difference reaches zero.
c0057: Nominal annual rate (not APR). The example (10%) is the kit's assumption for an SBA 7(a) loan. A smaller loan with a used van and kitchen equipment as collateral often prices above a storefront loan: ask two lenders for quotes, and ask about SBA-guaranteed loans, before you set it.
c0059: Total years, interest-only period included. A van and kitchen equipment lose value faster than a storefront build-out, so the term is shorter. SBA 7(a) allows up to 10 years for equipment and working capital.
c0061: ZERO by default: repayment starts in year 1, so the year-1 DSCR already measures the full loan payment. If you negotiate an interest-only first year, enter it here and read the year-1 DSCR with care.
c0063: The minimum this workbook asks for (see "Instructions"): a cushion below 3 months does not cover a slow stretch, such as the off-season for weddings or a corporate client who pays late.
c0079: The refrigerated van, its upfit (racks, shelving, wrap) and its refrigeration unit: everything mounted on the van is depreciated with it. Straight-line book depreciation; tax methods such as MACRS or Section 179 are separate, so confirm with your accountant.
c0081: Kitchen and refrigeration equipment, portable cooking and power, POS, smallwares and serving ware. Loading and unloading at every event wears them faster than a fixed kitchen, so a short life is prudent. Straight-line book depreciation; MACRS or Section 179 are tax treatments: confirm with your accountant.
c0087: INFORMATION ONLY: it does not enter any calculation in this workbook. It is your estimate of the most events a year your kitchen hours and crew can handle. Compare it with the events per year you plan and with the optimistic scenario: if the plan goes above it, you need more commissary hours or more staff. Volume itself is driven by the "Events per year" cell above.
c0089: A new caterer does not book in month one what it books in month eight: weddings are reserved months ahead and corporate clients want to try you first. Events per year above is the year-1 AVERAGE: the ramp only spreads year 1's sales across the months (slower start, stronger finish) and keeps the annual total. At 100% there is no ramp.
c0093: Getting the commissary agreement, the catering permit and the van ready takes weeks (see Phase 2 of your checklist), so you pay commissary rent before your first event. It belongs in startup costs, not in the P&L.
c0095: Calculated by formula on the van, upfit and fit-out lines: if you change the van price, the contingency recalculates on its own. The note on that row of the "Startup Costs" tab lists exactly which lines are included.
c0098: Average days between the event and the money in your bank. Weddings are usually prepaid and many companies pay at 30 days, so the example sits in between. Raise it if clients or marketplaces pay later. The workbook does not model deposits (25-50% at signing is common: Kit estimate): they improve your real cash flow.
c0106: ZERO by default: the client buys the alcohol and certified bartenders serve it, so you sell none. Selling alcohol requires a liquor license (and, in some states, an event-by-event caterer's permit): check your state before adding it. Keep liquor liability coverage whenever bartenders pour at your events.
c0108: Only used if you enter alcohol sales above, which is zero in this plan. Example rate: the same as the rest of the sales (state + local combined). Some states tax alcohol at a different rate or add liquor taxes: if you sell alcohol, enter the rate that applies.
c0117: Enter the minimum wage of your state or city, annualized for a full-time job (hourly rate × 2,080 hours). The pay floor in the "Staffing" tab is the HIGHER of this cell and the federal minimum. With 0 or blank, the traffic light compares only against the federal floor. Check current rates at dol.gov.
c0124: Enter a whole number from 1 to 365: guests per event or days.
c0144: A used refrigerated cargo van. Prices vary widely with size, mileage and condition, so get several quotes. A Transit-size van does not need a CDL (that starts at 26,001 lb GVWR).
c0147: Racks, shelving, tie-downs for hot boxes and carriers, and the vehicle wrap.
c0149: Ovens, range, reach-in refrigeration, prep tables and sinks that you own. If your commissary supplies its own equipment, lower this line.
c0151: Induction units and burners for stations, plus a quiet generator or battery power for venues without hookups.
c0153: Refrigeration unit for the cargo area, installed, to hold cold food at 41°F or below in transit.
c0155: Shelving, lockers and labeled bins for your dry and cold storage inside the commissary. Ask the kitchen what it already provides before you budget this line.
c0157: State filing fees for the articles of organization (Secretary of State) plus any attorney or filing-service fees; a registered agent is also needed. Fees vary a lot by state. The "Taxable / recoverable tax?" column is set to No: it only matters if you enter a recoverable input tax rate (for example UK VAT).
c0160: Varies a lot by city and county: get the amounts for yours before you close the budget. Expect the catering or health permit, the business license and the van inspection; temporary food event permits are charged per event on top.
c0162: Many counties review a caterer's written operating procedures before issuing the permit and charge a plan review fee (one California county does: eldoradocounty.ca.gov). If you lease your own kitchen, expect a full plan review with layout drawings, which costs more.
c0164: Catering software for quotes, contracts and invoices, plus a card reader to take deposits and final balances.
c0166: Hotel pans, sheet pans, utensils and cooking tools: the equipment that gets depreciated. Daily disposables are NOT depreciated: they go in the disposables line of the P&L, at the % of sales set in the "0. Assumptions" tab.
c0168: Food and supplies for your first events. With 0% recoverable input tax (the US default), any sales tax you pay on this purchase is treated as a cost.
c0170: Website, event photography, listings on The Knot, WeddingWire and ezCater, Google Business Profile and a launch tasting.
c0172: Chafing dishes, insulated food carriers, platters, serving utensils, linens and signage for buffets and stations.
c0204: Food sales (drop-off, buffets, plated and stations)
c0205: Food sold at your events: corporate drop-offs and buffets, weddings, parties and chef-attended stations. All of it carries cost of goods sold at the same food rate.
c0206: Beverage sales (coffee, iced tea, lemonade and soft drinks)
c0207: Non-alcoholic drinks sold with the menu. The client buys any alcohol, so there is no bar revenue.
c0221: The monthly amount is typed in "0. Assumptions"; here it is multiplied by twelve. It covers your commissary hours, storage and the van's parking spot, not storefront rent. The months before opening are on the "Startup Costs" tab and are NOT counted twice.
c0225: Generator and portable-burner fuel, plus water and utility costs that the commissary fee does not cover.
c0228: Annual permits and licenses (catering permit, business license)
c0234: Waste and grease disposal (organic waste, cardboard and used cooking oil)
c0235: Licensed hauler. Ask the commissary first: many include trash and grease pickup in the fee. If yours does not, get a quote in your area.
c0237: A licensed pest control company, usually arranged through the commissary. It is part of the HACCP-based food safety plan your checklist asks for in the staff phase.
c0239: Food handler cards and a Certified Food Protection Manager course for you and your team, alcohol server certification (TIPS or TABC) for the bartenders you staff, plus OSHA basics. The required cards vary by state.
c0241: Food cost and labor for the tastings you offer wedding and corporate prospects. Many caterers charge a fee and credit it toward the booking: if you do, lower this line.
c0265: Floor set by this workbook: kit benchmark (editable estimate). The workbook's gross margin also subtracts card fees, marketplace commissions and van fuel, so the floor sits below the 65-70% that caterer pricing guides quote on food cost alone.
c0268: Ceiling for food + beverage cost of goods (disposables have their own line): kit benchmark (editable estimate), based on the 28-35% food cost range for caterers in the benchmarks table.
c0270: Ceiling: kit benchmark (editable estimate), above the 25-35% labor range that pricing guides report because it includes the owner-chef's own pay.
c0272: There is no storefront rent in this workbook: 8% is a prudent ceiling for the commissary kitchen and van parking, a kit benchmark (editable estimate). A business with its own fixed kitchen carries a much higher occupancy cost.
c0274: Floor of 5%: a kit benchmark (editable estimate), a little below the 7-8% average net margin that caterers report (itsacheckmate.com). A new business with a loan to repay starts lower.
c0309: Events per year needed to cover costs for each price per guest (columns, in steps around the plan's price) and each variable cost per guest (rows). Green cells are below the events per year the plan forecasts.
c0310: Events per year needed: price per guest excl. sales tax (columns) × variable cost per guest (rows)
c0324: The SAME staffing in all three scenarios. In the pessimistic case your real event-staff cost falls with the number of events (you pay hours per event), so the real result would be somewhat better than shown. If labor cost still blows up, adjust it in the "Staffing" tab, not here
c0326: Guests each full-time equivalent in the "Staffing" table would have to serve in a year. In the optimistic scenario it tells you whether you need to hire
c0331: The "Base" column reads its three inputs (events per year, price per guest and guests per event) from the "0. Assumptions" tab, so it reproduces EXACTLY year 1 of the P&L. The other two scenarios use the same cost rates: only events, price and guests change. FIXED COSTS are the same in all three, while variable costs follow the sales of each scenario.
c0344: Sells, runs tastings, plans menus and leads the kitchen on event days. Covers the main shift at every event.
c0346: Leads prep and production in the commissary and runs the line at larger events. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0348: Servers, bartenders and attendants hired per event and paid hourly as W-2 employees. Their FTE is a fraction because they only work event hours. Treating them as 1099 contractors is a misclassification risk (FLSA; California AB5). Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0350: Preps in the commissary, loads the van and drives to venues. Paid at or above the pay floor in proportion to FTE.
c0360: 40 hours a week is the FLSA overtime threshold for non-exempt employees; some states add daily overtime rules. Change it if your own full-time week is different
c0364: Hours of work that one event needs: shopping, prep, loading, transport, setup, service, breakdown and cleanup. Serving is only part of it. Hours × people × events per year sets the event staff cost.
c0366: Average number of people working each event. A large wedding needs more hands: raise it here and the staffing sizes itself.
c0379: 1. "0. Assumptions" is the control sheet: events per year, price per guest excl. sales tax, guests per event, food and beverage mix, cost of goods sold, commissary kitchen and van parking, financing and taxes.
c0381: 3. Only "Break-Even" is derived entirely from the rest. The other three tabs also have green cells you can edit: the pessimistic and optimistic scenarios in "Scenarios", seasonality and the launch ramp-up in "12-Month Cash Flow", and the other funding sources in "Financing" (rows 8-11 count as sources but are not amortized: your bank or SBA 7(a) loan goes in "Loan requested" on "0. Assumptions"). Everything else is calculated.
c0386: 8. The Word business plan in this kit uses the same example figures as this workbook. The workbook is the one that recalculates on its own when you change a green cell: if you change one, update the matching figures in the Word document.
c0397: Events per year for the ACCOUNTING break-even (depreciation included)
c0404: A typed-in number that does not match the Staffing tab
c0405: Read directly from the Staffing tab
c0406: If you change a salary, the whole plan recalculates, so the P&L and the staffing table can never disagree.
c0408: One line called "staff", with no link to event hours or pay floors
c0409: Positions with their FTE, sized to the hours your events need, with event staff paid per event
c0410: A plan staffed for fewer hours than it sells does not work on its own numbers. This layout makes that gap visible before a lender does.
c0412: Sales typed as one lump sum, with no link to bookings
c0413: Revenue = events per year × guests per event × price per guest, one cell each for the whole workbook
c0414: Break-even, scenarios and the P&L read the same three cells, so they always agree, and you can see which lever moves the result: more events, bigger events or a higher price.
c0416: A price with no statement of whether sales tax or service is included
c0417: Declared EXCL. sales tax, with service included and the voluntary gratuity left out
c0418: Declaring it changes no number: it just says what the number is. Price per guest incl. sales tax = price per guest × (1 + sales tax rate), and the workbook calculates it for you.
c0420: Left out: the model shows no cost of space
c0421: A monthly commissary cost (hours + storage) and van parking, plus a deposit and rent for the months before opening
c0422: Catering has to be cooked in a permitted kitchen, not at home, so a commissary or shared kitchen is a real recurring cost. Leaving it out makes the business look like it has no occupancy cost.
c0424: A round number labeled "3 months" that does not match the fixed costs
c0425: Three months of cash fixed costs, calculated by formula
c0426: A round number often covers far less than the label says. This cushion is what keeps you open through a slow month between wedding seasons.
c0428: One useful life for everything, including items that are not fixed assets
c0429: Two useful lives: the van with its upfit, and the equipment and serving ware. The Startup Costs tab calculates the annual charge.
c0430: The van and the equipment wear out at different speeds. Working capital, opening inventory and launch marketing are not fixed assets, so they are not depreciated.
c0432: Counted twice: once in startup costs and again as an annual expense
c0433: Counted once, as an annual expense
c0434: Counting a premium in both places inflates the startup costs, the cash you need to raise and the loan you ask for.
c0436: A separate line, on top of utilities
c0438: Writing it in two places counts it twice: here it lives in one cell and the rest of the workbook follows.
c0440: A lump sum typed by hand
c0441: A percentage calculated on the van, upfit and fit-out lines
c0442: If you change the van price, the contingency recalculates instead of staying at the old amount.
c0444: A flat rate every year, with no offset for losses
c0445: One effective rate for years 1-2 and another from year 3, offsetting net operating losses carried forward
c0446: A loss in one year reduces taxable profit in later years. The model offsets losses fully as a simplification (federal rules cap the offset at 80% of taxable income). If you operate as a pass-through (sole proprietorship or LLC), set the rate to 0 and budget your personal tax separately.
c0448: The full payment deducted in the P&L
c0449: Only interest in the P&L; principal repaid in the cash flow
c0450: Putting the full payment above the line turns the P&L into a cash flow, and a lender spots it immediately.
c0453: A dedicated tab: where the money comes from, what it pays for and the amortization schedule year by year
c0454: It is the sheet a lender asks for next to the P&L, and it warns you when the money you put in falls short of what you need.
c0457: A 12-month tab: cash in, cash out, quarterly sales tax and the cumulative balance
c0458: It answers the one question that decides a loan: in which month does the business run out of cash?
c0460: Fuel and a miscellaneous line typed in among the fixed costs
c0461: One percentage of sales, treated as a variable cost
c0462: Fuel rises and falls with the number of events you cater: putting it among the fixed costs distorts the break-even.
c0463: Cost of goods on all sales
c0464: Revenue with no cost of goods sold attached
c0465: Every food sale carries cost of goods sold at the same rate, whatever the service style
c0466: A revenue line that pays for no ingredients shows a margin that does not exist.
c0468: Wages never compared with any legal floor
c0469: No row below the pay floor in proportion to its FTE, and a cell for your state or local minimum wage
c0470: State and local minimums are often higher than the federal one: enter yours in "0. Assumptions" and the traffic light warns you when a wage falls short.
c0479: High-end menus run about 25% and high-volume menus about 40%. The example sits inside the range: if your menu runs at 35%, year-1 profit gets very tight.
c0483: Before overhead. The workbook subtracts card fees, marketplace commissions and van fuel from it too, so its floor is set lower.
c0487: Kitchen, administration and part of the owner's time; itsacheckmate.com gives 20-35%. The workbook's ceiling is higher because it includes the owner-chef's pay.
c0491: Average for caterers. A new business with a loan to repay starts lower: improve it with more events, bigger events or a higher price per guest.
c0495: Average in 2024 (The Knot 2025 Real Weddings Study, via Fox Business). Your market, menu and service style move it a lot.
c0499: Typical event of 50-75 guests. Corporate drop-offs sit at the low end; plated dinners with staff at the high end.
c0503: Boxed lunches run about $12-$35+ and drop-off buffets about $20-$38 on published corporate catering menus. Check your local competitors.
c0507: ezCater lists about 15% on food and delivery, plus card processing. Fees change: check the current schedule before you count on a rate.
c0511: Common at signing, with the balance due 5-7 days before the event; companies often pay at 30 days. The workbook does not model deposits, so they improve your real cash flow.
c0515: Chef or manager $25-$35, prep cook $15-$18, servers and bartenders $18-$25. Add 15-30% for payroll taxes and benefits.
c0519: 2023 Shared Kitchen Operator Survey; 42% of operators charge $20-$29 per hour. Storage and parking cost extra.
c0523: With a shared kitchen; $250K+ if you build your own. Your total depends mostly on the van and the equipment you choose. The example ($107,200 before working capital) sits above this range because it buys a refrigerated van ($41,000 with its unit) and its own serving equipment.
c0527: Insureon averages for businesses under 5 employees: general liability, commercial auto and liquor liability. Your quotes will differ.
c0531: Rule of thumb: stations and heavy service need more hands. Use it to size the event staff row in the "Staffing" tab.
